claims.text: The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has high plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
High effective stacking-fault energy governs the low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
High stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation cross-slip during deformation.
Facile cross-slip allows dislocations to bypass obstacles without substantial interaction.
Facile cross-slip suppresses localized dislocation pile-ups and dislocation accumulation.
Facile cross-slip suppresses the activation of deformation twinning.
Dislocation pile-ups and deformation twins provide barriers to slip and can increase work hardening and strength.
A tailored heat treatment can induce slight compositional clustering or nanoscale ordering without forming a secondary phase.
The proposed clustering or ordering will raise the barrier to cross-slip and promote dislocation accumulation or twin nucleation.
Constrained dislocation motion and increased twin formation create effective internal barriers to dislocation glide.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the heat-treated CoCrFeNiTi alloy will have higher yield strength and hardness.
The heat-treated alloy will exhibit fewer cross-slip events and more dislocation pile-up or deformation twins.
The proposed microstructural changes will produce a greater work-hardening response.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC CoCrFeNiTi at room temperature and moderate strain rates.
Phase transformations or precipitate formation could independently affect the mechanical properties and therefore must be avoided.
The quantitative effect of Ti on stacking-fault energy and dislocation dynamics in CoCrFeNiTi is not established by the cited evidence.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant strength or hardness increase, or failure to observe reduced cross-slip with increased twinning or pile-up, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
